01_Atoms_elements_and_compounds_the_basi.title: Atoms, elements and compounds — the basics
01_Atoms_elements_and_compounds_the_basi.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Define the terms atom, element, compound and mixture.
Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures using particle diagrams.
Explain the difference between a chemical change and a physical change.

theory_blocks.title: Everything is made of atoms
theory_blocks.body:
Every substance you can see, touch or smell is built from atoms — unimaginably small particles that cannot be broken apart by chemical means. A single grain of sand contains about 50 000 000 000 000 000 000 atoms.

An **element** is a substance made from only one type of atom. Iron is an element because every atom in a piece of iron is an iron atom. Oxygen is an element because it contains only oxygen atoms.

There are about 118 known elements. The periodic table organises them all by their properties and the structure of their atoms.

theory_blocks.title: Compounds and mixtures
theory_blocks.body:
A **compound** is a substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements are chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Water (H₂O) is a compound: every water molecule contains exactly two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

Key properties of compounds:
• They have a **fixed composition** — the ratio of atoms is always the same.
• Their properties are **different from the elements** that make them. Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a toxic gas, but sodium chloride (table salt) is safe to eat.
• They can only be separated back into their elements by **chemical reactions**, not by physical methods.

A **mixture** contains two or more substances that are not chemically bonded. The substances keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, distillation or chromatography.

Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon and other gases. Salt water is a mixture of sodium chloride and water.

theory_blocks.title: Chemical changes versus physical changes
theory_blocks.body:
In a **physical change**, no new substance is formed. The particles stay the same — only their arrangement or energy changes. Melting ice and dissolving sugar in water are physical changes.

In a **chemical change** (a chemical reaction), new substances are formed. The atoms rearrange to make different molecules or structures. Burning magnesium in air, an iron nail rusting, and baking a cake are all chemical changes.

Signs that a chemical change has occurred include:
• a colour change (that is not just mixing or dissolving)
• a gas being produced (bubbles or fizzing)
• a temperature change (getting hotter or colder)
• a new solid forming (a precipitate)
• a change that is difficult or impossible to reverse

Note: these signs are evidence, not proof — some physical changes also involve temperature or colour changes.

theory_blocks.title: Reading particle diagrams
theory_blocks.body:
Particle diagrams use small circles to represent atoms. Each type of atom is drawn in a different colour or size.

• If all circles are the same → **element** (all atoms identical).
• If circles of different types are joined together, and every group looks the same → **compound** (fixed ratio of bonded atoms).
• If there are separate circles of different types, or groups AND single circles that are not bonded → **mixture**.

Exam tip: always check whether different atom types are **bonded together** (compound) or **just mixed** (mixture). Two different-coloured circles next to each other but not bonded is a mixture, not a compound.

keywords.definition: The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
A substance made from only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
A substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements are chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio.
Two or more substances that are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods.

worked_examples.statement: Classify each of the following as an element, compound or mixture: (a) pure iron, (b) carbon dioxide, (c) air, (d) distilled water.
knowns: air contains N₂, O₂, Ar and other gases
worked_examples.solution:
(a) **Iron** — element. It contains only one type of atom (Fe).
(b) **Carbon dioxide** — compound. It contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (CO₂).
(c) **Air** — mixture. It contains several different gases that are not chemically bonded to each other and can be separated by fractional distillation.
(d) **Distilled water** — compound. It contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (H₂O).
worked_examples.interpretation: An element has one type of atom; a compound has two or more types chemically bonded; a mixture has substances not chemically bonded.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Confusing air with a compound because 'it is all around us' — air is a mixture of separate gases.

worked_examples.statement: For each process, decide whether it is a chemical change or a physical change and explain your reasoning: (a) melting butter, (b) burning wood, (c) dissolving salt in water.
unknowns: Whether each is chemical or physical
worked_examples.solution:
(a) **Melting butter** — physical change. The butter changes from solid to liquid, but no new substance is formed. It can be re-solidified by cooling.
(b) **Burning wood** — chemical change. New substances (carbon dioxide, water vapour, ash) are formed. The process cannot be reversed.
(c) **Dissolving salt in water** — physical change. The salt particles separate and spread through the water, but no new substance is formed. The salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
worked_examples.interpretation: Chemical changes produce new substances; physical changes only alter the state or arrangement.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Thinking dissolving is a chemical change because the solid 'disappears'. The salt is still NaCl — its particles are just spread out among the water molecules.

exercises.statement: State two differences between a compound and a mixture.
exercises.answer: 1. In a compound, atoms of different elements are chemically bonded together; in a mixture, the substances are not chemically bonded. 2. A compound has a fixed composition (ratio of atoms); a mixture can have varying proportions.
exercises.full_solution: A compound has a fixed composition and its components are chemically bonded, so it can only be separated by chemical reactions. A mixture has variable composition and its components are not chemically bonded, so it can be separated by physical methods.

common_errors.correction: Mixtures can contain elements, compounds or both.

exercises.statement: A particle diagram shows the following: groups of three identical circles arranged in triangles, with no other types of circle present. Is this an element, a compound or a mixture? Explain your answer.
exercises.answer: It is an element. All the circles (atoms) are identical — there is only one type of atom present. The groups of three represent molecules of the element (for example, ozone O₃ has three oxygen atoms bonded together).
exercises.full_solution: Since every circle is the same type, only one kind of atom is present, which defines an element. The triangular grouping means the atoms form molecules (like O₃), but since all atoms are the same element, the substance is still classified as an element, not a compound.

common_errors.error: Calling it a compound because the atoms are joined in groups
common_errors.correction: A compound requires atoms of different elements. Here all atoms are the same.

exercises.statement: When hydrochloric acid is added to zinc metal, bubbles of gas are produced and the zinc gradually dissolves. (a) Give two pieces of evidence from the description that suggest this is a chemical change. (b) Name the gas produced.
exercises.answer: (a) A gas is produced (bubbles) and the zinc dissolves / disappears — a new substance is formed. (b) Hydrogen gas.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Two pieces of evidence: (1) Gas production — the bubbles show a new gaseous substance is being formed. (2) The zinc dissolves — it is being converted into a different substance (zinc chloride in solution). Both indicate new products are formed, which is the hallmark of a chemical change.
(b) The gas is hydrogen (H₂). When a metal reacts with an acid, the products are a salt and hydrogen gas.

common_errors.error: Naming the gas as oxygen or carbon dioxide
common_errors.correction: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Carbon dioxide is produced when a carbonate reacts with acid.

exercises.statement: Define the following terms: (a) atom, (b) element, (c) compound, (d) mixture.
exercises.answer: (a) An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. (b) An element is a substance made of only one type of atom. (c) A compound is a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together. (d) A mixture is two or more substances not chemically combined.

exercises.statement: State whether each of the following is an element, compound or mixture: (a) oxygen gas O₂, (b) carbon dioxide CO₂, (c) air, (d) pure water H₂O, (e) bronze.
exercises.answer: (a) Element — only oxygen atoms. (b) Compound — carbon and oxygen chemically bonded. (c) Mixture — several gases not chemically combined. (d) Compound — hydrogen and oxygen chemically bonded. (e) Mixture — copper and tin metals mixed (alloy) but not chemically bonded in a compound.

exercises.statement: A particle diagram shows four identical pairs of joined circles scattered among single circles of a different colour. (a) Is this diagram showing an element, compound or mixture? (b) Explain your reasoning.
exercises.answer: (a) Mixture. (b) There are two types of particle: diatomic molecules (pairs of the same atom) and separate single atoms of a different element. Since these are not chemically bonded to each other, this is a mixture of an element (diatomic molecules) and another element (single atoms).

challenge_questions.statement:
(a) A student looks at five particle diagrams and must classify each as an element, compound or mixture. Diagram A shows identical diatomic molecules; Diagram B shows a lattice of alternating ions; Diagram C shows two different types of single atoms mixed randomly. Classify each and justify your answer. (3 marks)
(b) The student claims that Diagram A must be a compound because the atoms are joined. Explain why this reasoning is incorrect. (2 marks)
(c) Give one example of a substance that matches each diagram type. (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Diagram A: element — all atoms are the same element, bonded as diatomic molecules (e.g. O₂). Diagram B: compound — two different elements bonded in a regular lattice (e.g. NaCl). Diagram C: mixture — two types of atoms not chemically bonded together.
(b) The student is wrong because a compound requires atoms of at least two different elements chemically bonded. Diagram A shows atoms of the same element bonded together, which makes it a molecular element, not a compound.
(c) A: O₂ or H₂; B: NaCl or MgO; C: air or a mixture of iron and sulfur powders.

challenge_questions.statement:
Iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed together. A student heats part of the mixture strongly until it glows.
(a) Before heating, explain how you could separate the iron from the sulfur. (2 marks)
(b) After heating, the product is a grey-black solid that does not attract a magnet. Explain why a magnet no longer works. (2 marks)
(c) Write a word equation for the reaction and state the type of change. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Use a magnet to attract the iron filings and leave the sulfur behind, because iron is magnetic but sulfur is not.
(b) A chemical reaction has occurred forming iron sulfide (FeS). The iron atoms are now chemically bonded to sulfur atoms in a compound, so the iron is no longer in its elemental metallic form and loses its magnetic property.
(c) Iron + sulfur → iron sulfide. This is a chemical change because a new substance with different properties is formed.

challenge_questions.statement:
A student says: 'When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar undergoes a chemical change because it disappears.'
(a) Explain why the student is incorrect. (2 marks)
(b) Describe one test the student could do to prove it is a physical change. (2 marks)
(c) Give two observable signs that would indicate a chemical change has actually occurred in a different reaction. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Dissolving is a physical change because the sugar molecules are still intact — they are just dispersed among water molecules. No new substance is formed.
(b) The student could gently evaporate the water from the solution. If it is a physical change, the sugar crystals will be left behind, proving the sugar was not destroyed.
(c) Any two of: colour change, gas bubbles produced, temperature change, precipitate formed, light/sound emitted.

mcq.stem: Which of the following is a compound?

options.why_wrong: Oxygen gas contains only oxygen atoms. Although the atoms are bonded in pairs, it is an element because only one type of atom is present.
Bronze is a mixture (an alloy) of copper and tin atoms. They are not chemically bonded in a fixed ratio like a compound.
Air is a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, etc.) that are not chemically bonded together.

mcq.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is a compound because it contains atoms of two different elements (sodium and chlorine) chemically bonded together in a fixed 1:1 ratio.

mcq.stem: A particle diagram shows large dark circles and small light circles joined together in identical pairs. The diagram represents:

options.why_wrong: The circles are different sizes/colours, meaning two types of atom are present. An element has only one type.
The different atoms are joined (bonded) together in pairs, not separate. Bonded different atoms = compound.
All the groups are identical pairs of two different atoms — this is one compound, not a mixture.

mcq.explanation: The diagram shows atoms of two different elements bonded together in a fixed ratio (pairs), which defines a compound.

mcq.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that a chemical change has occurred?

options.text: The substance changes from a solid to a liquid
options.why_wrong: Melting is a physical change — no new substance forms.

options.text: The substance dissolves to give a colourless solution
options.why_wrong: Dissolving is usually a physical change — the substance spreads through the solvent but remains the same substance.

options.text: A new solid forms at the bottom of the test tube and the temperature rises
The substance changes colour when crushed into powder
options.why_wrong: Crushing is a physical change; the colour change may be due to different light reflection from smaller particles.

mcq.explanation: Formation of a new solid (precipitate) together with a temperature change is strong evidence of a chemical reaction producing new substances. Multiple signs together are stronger evidence than one sign alone.

mcq.stem: What is the correct definition of an atom?

options.text: The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction
A substance that cannot be broken down by chemical reactions
options.why_wrong: This describes an element, not an atom.

options.text: Two or more elements chemically combined
options.why_wrong: This describes a compound, not an atom.

options.text: The smallest particle that can exist on its own
options.why_wrong: Some atoms cannot exist independently in normal conditions. Also, molecules can be smaller than some atoms.

mcq.explanation: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. This is the standard GCSE definition.

exam_notes.note: Learn the exact definitions of atom, element, compound and mixture — these are frequently tested as define/state questions worth 1–2 marks.
In particle diagram questions, check whether different circles are bonded (touching/overlapping) or separate.

summary.big_idea: All matter is made from atoms. Elements contain one type of atom, compounds have different atoms bonded together, and mixtures are substances not chemically combined.
key_points: An atom is the smallest particle of an element.
Compounds have a fixed ratio of bonded atoms from different elements.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods; compounds require chemical reactions.
Chemical changes form new substances; physical changes do not.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Elements = one atom type. Compounds = different atoms bonded. Mixtures = substances not bonded.

theory_blocks.title: Atomic number and mass number
theory_blocks.body:
Every atom has a tiny, dense centre called the **nucleus**, which contains **protons** (positive charge) and **neutrons** (no charge). Orbiting the nucleus are **electrons** (negative charge).

Two numbers identify each element:

**Atomic number (Z)** = the number of protons in the nucleus.
• This defines which element the atom is. All carbon atoms have 6 protons; all oxygen atoms have 8.
• In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

**Mass number (A)** = protons + neutrons.
• This is the total number of particles in the nucleus.
• You can calculate the number of neutrons: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

On the periodic table, each element's box typically shows:
• The element's **symbol** (e.g. Na for sodium)
• The **atomic number** (smaller number, usually above)
• The **relative atomic mass** (larger number, often below) — this is close to the mass number but is a weighted average of all isotopes.

theory_blocks.title: Groups, periods and organisation
theory_blocks.body:
The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number.

**Periods** are the horizontal rows (1 to 7). As you go across a period from left to right:
• The atomic number increases by 1 each time.
• Elements change from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.

**Groups** are the vertical columns. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

Key groups to know:
• **Group 1** — alkali metals (Li, Na, K…): very reactive metals, react with water.
• **Group 7** — halogens (F, Cl, Br, I…): reactive non-metals, form salts with metals.
• **Group 0 (or 18)** — noble gases (He, Ne, Ar…): very unreactive, full outer shell.

The dividing line between metals and non-metals runs diagonally from boron to astatine.

theory_blocks.title: Finding information from the periodic table
theory_blocks.body:
Suppose you look up sodium (Na) in the periodic table and see:
• Atomic number: 11
• Relative atomic mass: 23.0
• Group 1, Period 3

From these numbers you can work out:
• Protons = 11 (same as atomic number)
• Electrons = 11 (equals protons in a neutral atom)
• Neutrons ≈ 23 − 11 = 12 (mass number minus atomic number)
• It is in Group 1, so it has 1 electron in its outer shell
• It is in Period 3, so it has 3 occupied electron shells
• It is a metal (left side of the table) in the alkali metals group

worked_examples.statement: Use the periodic table to find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in an atom of aluminium (Al). Aluminium has atomic number 13 and relative atomic mass 27.0.
unknowns: Number of protons, electrons and neutrons
worked_examples.solution:
Protons = atomic number = **13**
Electrons = protons (neutral atom) = **13**
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = **14**
worked_examples.interpretation: The atomic number always gives protons directly. For a neutral atom, electrons = protons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the relative atomic mass without rounding — for calculating neutrons, round Ar to the nearest whole number to get the mass number.

worked_examples.statement: Potassium (K) is in Group 1, Period 4. Predict two chemical properties of potassium based on its position.
worked_examples.solution:
1. Potassium is a very reactive metal — Group 1 elements are the alkali metals, which react vigorously with water.
2. Potassium has 1 electron in its outer shell (Group 1), so it will easily lose this electron to form a K⁺ ion with a +1 charge.
worked_examples.interpretation: The group number tells you the number of outer-shell electrons and predicts reactivity patterns.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Confusing group number with the total number of electrons. Group number = outer shell electrons only.

exercises.statement: Define the terms 'atomic number' and 'mass number'.
exercises.answer: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
exercises.full_solution: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. It defines which element the atom is. Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons. It gives the total number of nucleons.

common_errors.error: Saying mass number is the mass of the atom
common_errors.correction: Mass number is the count of protons + neutrons, not a mass in grams.

exercises.statement: Chlorine has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. Calculate the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in a neutral chlorine atom.
exercises.answer: Protons = 17, Electrons = 17, Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.
exercises.full_solution: Protons = atomic number = 17. Electrons = protons (since the atom is neutral) = 17. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 35 − 17 = 18.

common_errors.correction: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = atomic number, not mass number.

exercises.statement: Element X is in Group 7, Period 3 of the periodic table. (a) How many electrons does it have in its outer shell? (b) Is it a metal or a non-metal? (c) Name element X.
exercises.answer: (a) 7 electrons in the outer shell. (b) Non-metal. (c) Chlorine.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Group 7 means 7 electrons in the outer shell. (b) Group 7 elements are non-metals (halogens). (c) Period 3 and Group 7 identifies the element as chlorine (Cl, atomic number 17).

common_errors.correction: Group 7 (halogens) are non-metals. Metals are on the left side of the periodic table.

exercises.statement: Use the periodic table to find the following for magnesium (Mg): (a) atomic number, (b) mass number, (c) number of protons, (d) number of electrons, (e) group and period.
exercises.answer: (a) 12. (b) 24. (c) 12. (d) 12. (e) Group II, Period 3.

exercises.statement: State the electronic configuration for: (a) lithium (Z = 3), (b) carbon (Z = 6), (c) neon (Z = 10), (d) sodium (Z = 11).
Element Y has 17 protons. (a) Write its electronic configuration. (b) State its group and period. (c) Predict whether it is a metal or non-metal.
exercises.answer: (a) 2,8,7. (b) Group VII, Period 3. (c) Non-metal (it is chlorine, in the halogen group on the right side of the periodic table).

challenge_questions.statement:
Element X has an atomic number of 12 and a mass number of 24.
(a) State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom of X. (3 marks)
(b) Identify element X and state which group and period it belongs to. (2 marks)
(c) Another isotope of X has a mass number of 25. Explain what is meant by the term 'isotope' and state how this atom differs from the one in part (a). (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Protons = 12, Neutrons = 24 − 12 = 12, Electrons = 12.
(b) Element X is magnesium (Mg). It is in Group II, Period 3.
(c) Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. The isotope with mass number 25 has 13 neutrons instead of 12, but still has 12 protons and 12 electrons.

challenge_questions.statement:
The periodic table shows that chlorine has a relative atomic mass of 35.5, even though mass numbers must be whole numbers.
(a) Explain why the relative atomic mass is not a whole number. (2 marks)
(b) Chlorine has two isotopes: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. If the relative atomic mass is 35.5, deduce the approximate percentage abundance of each isotope. (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) The relative atomic mass is an average of the masses of all the isotopes of chlorine, weighted by their natural abundances. Since it is an average, it does not have to be a whole number.
(b) Let x = fraction of ³⁵Cl. Then (35 × x) + (37 × (1 − x)) = 35.5. Solving: 35x + 37 − 37x = 35.5 → −2x = −1.5 → x = 0.75. So ³⁵Cl ≈ 75% and ³⁷Cl ≈ 25%.

challenge_questions.statement:
A student looks up three elements: sodium (Na), silicon (Si) and chlorine (Cl).
(a) Classify each as a metal or non-metal. (1 mark)
(b) Predict which would have the highest melting point and explain your reasoning using ideas about structure. (3 marks)
(c) Predict which would conduct electricity and explain why. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Na = metal; Si = non-metal (metalloid); Cl = non-metal.
(b) Silicon has the highest melting point because it has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice that require a lot of energy to break. Na has metallic bonding (moderate m.p.) and Cl₂ has weak intermolecular forces (very low m.p.).
(c) Sodium conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge. Silicon is a semiconductor. Chlorine does not conduct as it has no free electrons or ions.

theory_blocks.title: Reading chemical formulas
theory_blocks.body:
A **chemical formula** uses element symbols and subscript numbers to show which elements are in a compound and how many atoms of each.

**Rules for reading formulas:**
1. Each capital letter starts a new element symbol: CO₂ contains C and O (not Co, which is cobalt).
2. A subscript number after a symbol shows how many atoms of that element: H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
3. No subscript means 1 atom.
4. Brackets with a subscript multiply everything inside: Ca(OH)₂ has 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H.

**State symbols** show the physical state:
• (s) = solid
• (l) = liquid
• (g) = gas
• (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water)

Example: NaCl(s) means solid sodium chloride.

**Common formulas to know:**
• Water: H₂O
• Carbon dioxide: CO₂
• Hydrochloric acid: HCl
• Sodium hydroxide: NaOH
• Sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄

theory_blocks.title: Word equations and symbol equations
theory_blocks.body:
A **word equation** names the reactants and products of a reaction:

    magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide

• **Reactants** are on the left of the arrow (the starting substances).
• **Products** are on the right of the arrow (the new substances formed).
• The arrow means 'reacts to form'.
• A '+' sign between substances means 'and'.

A **symbol equation** uses chemical formulas instead of names:

    2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)

• The large number in front of a formula (the **coefficient**) shows how many units of that substance are involved.
• 2Mg means 2 atoms of magnesium; 2MgO means 2 formula units of magnesium oxide.
• The total number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides — this is a **balanced** equation.

Word equations are useful for describing what happens; symbol equations give the exact amounts and can be used for calculations.

theory_blocks.title: Counting atoms in a formula
theory_blocks.body:
**Example:** How many atoms of each element are in Ca(OH)₂?

Step 1: The bracket contains O and H. The subscript 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside.
Step 2: Ca: 1 atom (no subscript).
Step 3: O: 1 × 2 = 2 atoms.
Step 4: H: 1 × 2 = 2 atoms.

**Total: 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H = 5 atoms altogether.**

**Example:** How many atoms in 2H₂SO₄?

Step 1: The coefficient 2 multiplies the whole formula.
Step 2: H: 2 × 2 = 4 atoms.
Step 3: S: 1 × 2 = 2 atoms.
Step 4: O: 4 × 2 = 8 atoms.

**Total: 4 H, 2 S, 8 O = 14 atoms altogether.**

worked_examples.statement: How many atoms of each element are in one formula unit of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃?

worked_examples.solution:
Al: 2 atoms (subscript 2 after Al).
S: 1 × 3 = 3 atoms (1 S inside the bracket, multiplied by 3 outside).
O: 4 × 3 = 12 atoms (4 O inside the bracket, multiplied by 3 outside).

Total: 2 Al, 3 S, 12 O = 17 atoms.
worked_examples.interpretation: Brackets multiply everything inside. Work through each element systematically.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply the S by 3 — the subscript outside the bracket applies to all atoms inside.

worked_examples.statement: When sodium reacts with water, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas are produced. Write the word equation for this reaction.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reactants go on the left of the arrow, products on the right. Use '+' between multiple reactants or products.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reversing reactants and products. Remember: the starting substances are always on the left.

exercises.statement: How many atoms of each element are in Mg(NO₃)₂?
exercises.answer: Mg: 1, N: 2, O: 6. Total = 9 atoms.
exercises.full_solution: Mg: 1 (no subscript). The bracket (NO₃) is multiplied by 2: N = 1 × 2 = 2 atoms; O = 3 × 2 = 6 atoms. Total: 1 + 2 + 6 = 9 atoms.

common_errors.correction: The subscript 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside: O = 3 × 2 = 6.

exercises.statement: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid to form zinc chloride and hydrogen. Write the word equation.
exercises.answer: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
exercises.full_solution: Reactants: zinc and hydrochloric acid (left side). Products: zinc chloride and hydrogen (right side). The arrow represents 'reacts to form'.

common_errors.error: Using an equals sign instead of an arrow
common_errors.correction: Chemical equations use → (or →) not = between reactants and products.

exercises.statement: In the equation 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g), identify: (a) the reactants, (b) the products, (c) the state of sodium hydroxide, (d) the total number of hydrogen atoms on each side.
exercises.answer: (a) Sodium and water. (b) Sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. (c) Aqueous (dissolved in water). (d) Left: 2 × 2 = 4 H atoms; Right: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2 = 4 H atoms. Both sides have 4 hydrogen atoms.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Reactants (left of arrow): Na and H₂O. (b) Products (right of arrow): NaOH and H₂. (c) NaOH(aq) — the (aq) means aqueous, dissolved in water. (d) Left: 2H₂O contains 2 × 2 = 4 H. Right: 2NaOH has 2 × 1 = 2 H, and H₂ has 2 H, giving 2 + 2 = 4 H. The equation is balanced for hydrogen.

common_errors.error: Missing the coefficient when counting atoms
common_errors.correction: 2H₂O means 2 molecules, each with 2 H atoms, so 2 × 2 = 4 H total.

exercises.statement: Write the chemical formula for: (a) water, (b) carbon dioxide, (c) sodium chloride, (d) calcium carbonate, (e) sulfuric acid.
exercises.answer: (a) H₂O. (b) CO₂. (c) NaCl. (d) CaCO₃. (e) H₂SO₄.

Write a word equation for: (a) the combustion of methane in oxygen, (b) the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid.
exercises.answer: (a) Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. (b) Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen.

challenge_questions.statement:
Consider the formula Ca(OH)₂.
(a) State the number of each type of atom present in one formula unit. (2 marks)
(b) A student writes the formula of calcium hydroxide as CaOH₂. Explain the error. (2 marks)
(c) Write a balanced equation for the reaction of calcium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, including state symbols. (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Ca: 1, O: 2, H: 2.
(b) CaOH₂ implies 1 oxygen and 2 hydrogens directly bonded, which is incorrect. The brackets in Ca(OH)₂ show there are two complete OH⁻ groups, giving 2 oxygens and 2 hydrogens.
(c) Ca(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

challenge_questions.statement:
Balance the following equations and identify the type of reaction in each case.
(a) Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂ (2 marks)
(b) CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (2 marks)
(c) For the reaction in (a), explain why it is classified as a redox reaction. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ — reduction (of iron oxide).
(b) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O — combustion.
(c) It is a redox reaction because iron(III) oxide is reduced (oxygen is removed from Fe₂O₃ to form Fe) while carbon monoxide is oxidised (oxygen is added to CO to form CO₂). Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.

challenge_questions.statement:
A student attempts to balance: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. They write: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂.
(a) Explain why this equation is not balanced. (1 mark)
(b) Write the correctly balanced equation with state symbols. (2 marks)
(c) Describe what you would observe during this reaction. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) On the left there is 1 Na and on the right 1 Na, but there are 2 H on the left and 3 H on the right (1 in OH and 2 in H₂), so hydrogen is not balanced.
(b) 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
(c) The sodium would fizz vigorously on the water surface, moving around. The solution would become warm. A squeaky pop test with a lighted splint would confirm hydrogen gas.

theory_blocks.title: Why equations must balance
theory_blocks.body:
In every chemical reaction, atoms are **rearranged** but never created or destroyed. This is the **law of conservation of mass**: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.

This means a correct equation must have **exactly the same number of each type of atom** on both sides of the arrow. An unbalanced equation breaks this law.

For example, the unbalanced equation:
    H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
has 2 H and 2 O on the left, but 2 H and only 1 O on the right. The oxygen atoms don't match.

The balanced equation is:
    2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Now both sides have 4 H and 2 O. No atoms are gained or lost.

theory_blocks.title: How to balance an equation — step by step
theory_blocks.body:
**Step 1:** Write the correct formulas for all reactants and products. Never change a subscript to balance — that would create a different substance.

**Step 2:** Count the atoms of each element on both sides.

**Step 3:** Balance one element at a time by placing coefficients (large numbers) in front of formulas. Start with the element that appears in the fewest formulas, or save hydrogen and oxygen for last.

**Step 4:** Re-count after each change — adjusting one coefficient may unbalance another element.

**Step 5:** Check that every element has the same count on both sides.

**Step 6:** Make sure all coefficients are the smallest possible whole numbers (e.g. 2:1:2, not 4:2:4).

**Golden rule:** Only change coefficients (the big numbers in front), NEVER change subscripts (the small numbers within formulas).

theory_blocks.title: Worked example: balancing Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃
theory_blocks.body:
Balance: Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃

**Count atoms (unbalanced):**
  Left: Fe = 1, O = 2
  Right: Fe = 2, O = 3

**Step 1 — Balance Fe:** Put 2 in front of Fe:
  2Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃
  Fe: 2 = 2 ✓   O: 2 ≠ 3 ✗

**Step 2 — Balance O:** O appears as O₂ (multiples of 2) on the left and in groups of 3 on the right. The lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6.
  Left: need 6 O → put 3 in front of O₂: 3O₂ = 6 O
  Right: need 6 O → put 2 in front of Fe₂O₃: 2Fe₂O₃ = 6 O

  2Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃

**Step 3 — Re-check Fe:** Left: 2 Fe, Right: 2 × 2 = 4 Fe — not balanced!
  Fix: put 4 in front of Fe:
  4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃

**Final check:**
  Fe: 4 = 2 × 2 = 4 ✓
  O: 3 × 2 = 6 = 2 × 3 = 6 ✓

**Balanced equation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃**

theory_blocks.title: Why we need the mole
theory_blocks.body:
Atoms are far too small to count individually. Even a tiny grain of table salt contains billions of billions of ions. Chemists need a way to connect the invisible world of atoms to the measurable world of grams on a balance.

The **mole** is that bridge. One mole of any substance contains exactly **6.02 × 10²³** particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units). This number is called the **Avogadro constant** ($N_A$).

Why this particular number? Because it is chosen so that:
• 1 mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass of exactly 12 g.
• 1 mole of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass ($A_r$).

So the mole converts between 'number of particles' and 'mass in grams'.

Think of it like buying eggs by the dozen. A 'dozen' is always 12, whether they are small eggs or large eggs. A 'mole' is always 6.02 × 10²³, whether the particles are light (hydrogen) or heavy (lead).

theory_blocks.title: Molar mass and the mole formula
theory_blocks.body:
The **molar mass** ($M$) of a substance is the mass of one mole, measured in g/mol.

For an element: $M$ = relative atomic mass ($A_r$) in g/mol.
• $M$(Na) = 23.0 g/mol
• $M$(O) = 16.0 g/mol

For a compound: $M$ = relative formula mass ($M_r$) in g/mol.
Calculate $M_r$ by adding up the $A_r$ of every atom in the formula.

Example: $M_r$(H₂O) = (2 × 1.0) + (1 × 16.0) = 18.0, so $M$ = 18.0 g/mol.

The **mole formula** connects moles, mass and molar mass:

$$n = \frac{m}{M}$$

where:
• $n$ = number of moles (mol)
• $m$ = mass of the substance (g)
• $M$ = molar mass (g/mol)

Rearranged:
• $m = n \times M$ (to find mass)
• $M = \frac{m}{n}$ (to find molar mass)

Exam tip: In GCSE calculations, use the $A_r$ values given in the question or from the periodic table. These are often rounded (e.g. Cl = 35.5, Fe = 56).

theory_blocks.title: Worked example: calculating Mr and moles
theory_blocks.body:
**Example 1: Find Mr of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.**
$A_r$: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16.
$M_r$ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 40 + 12 + 48 = **100**
So 1 mole of CaCO₃ has a mass of 100 g.

**Example 2: How many moles are in 11 g of CO₂?**
Step 1: Calculate $M_r$(CO₂) = 12 + (2 × 16) = 44 g/mol.
Step 2: Use $n = m/M = 11/44 = **0.25 mol**$.

**Example 3: What mass of NaOH is needed for 0.5 mol?**
Step 1: $M_r$(NaOH) = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol.
Step 2: $m = n \times M = 0.5 \times 40 = **20 g**$.

worked_examples.statement: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄. (Ar: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)

challenge_questions.statement:
The Avogadro constant is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
(a) Define the term 'one mole of a substance'. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the number of molecules in 0.5 mol of water (H₂O). (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the total number of atoms in 0.5 mol of water. (2 marks)
(d) A student says '1 mole of any gas takes up the same volume.' State the conditions under which this is true and give the value of this volume. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) One mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.).
(b) 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.
(c) Each water molecule contains 3 atoms (2H + 1O), so total atoms = 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³ atoms.
(d) This is true at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), approximately 20 °C and 1 atm. The molar volume is 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ (or 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹).

challenge_questions.statement:
(a) Calculate the relative formula mass (Mᵣ) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16) (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of CaCO₃. (1 mark)
(c) A sample of calcium carbonate has a mass of 5.0 g. Calculate the number of moles. (2 marks)
(d) How many oxygen atoms are present in this sample? (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Mᵣ = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100.
(b) Mass = mol × Mᵣ = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.
(c) Moles = mass ÷ Mᵣ = 5.0 ÷ 100 = 0.05 mol.
(d) Each formula unit of CaCO₃ contains 3 oxygen atoms. Number of O atoms = 0.05 × 6.02 × 10²³ × 3 = 9.03 × 10²² atoms.

challenge_questions.statement: Explain, using the idea of moles, why 2 g of hydrogen gas (H₂) contains the same number of molecules as 32 g of oxygen gas (O₂). (Aᵣ: H = 1, O = 16) (4 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
Mᵣ of H₂ = 2 × 1 = 2. Moles of H₂ = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 mol.
Mᵣ of O₂ = 2 × 16 = 32. Moles of O₂ = 32 ÷ 32 = 1 mol.
Both samples contain 1 mole, which means both contain 6.02 × 10²³ molecules. One mole of any substance always contains the same number of particles (the Avogadro constant), regardless of what the substance is.

options.why_wrong: The Avogadro constant counts particles, not grams. The mass of one mole depends on the substance.
One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles — far more than 1.

mcq.explanation: One mole contains exactly 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant). This is true for all substances — the mass differs, but the count is always the same.

mcq.stem: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂? (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16, H = 1)

options.why_wrong: This is Mg + O + H = 24 + 16 + 1 = 41. You forgot to multiply by 2 for the bracket.
This would be 24 + 2(16+16+1) — you doubled the O subscript too, which is wrong.
This is just Mg + O = 24 + 16. You forgot H and the bracket multiplier.

options.why_wrong: 4.4 ÷ 12 = 0.37 — this uses the Ar of C alone, not the Mr of CO₂.
44/4.4 = 10 — you divided M by m instead of m by M.
4.4 ÷ 16 = 0.275 — this uses the Ar of O, not the Mr of CO₂.

options.why_wrong: 18 g is the mass of 1 mole, not 3 moles.

objectives.statement: Name and draw standard laboratory equipment including beaker, conical flask, measuring cylinder, burette, pipette, evaporating basin, crucible, Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze, clamp stand, filter funnel and boiling tube.

theory_blocks.title: Common laboratory equipment
theory_blocks.body:
**Measuring and containing:**
• **Beaker** — general-purpose container for liquids. Approximate volume markings.
• **Conical (Erlenmeyer) flask** — narrow neck reduces splashing when swirling.
• **Measuring cylinder** — reads liquid volumes accurately (read the meniscus at eye level).
• **Burette** — measures precise volumes delivered from a tap (used in titrations, accurate to ±0.05 cm³).
• **Pipette** — delivers a fixed, precise volume (e.g. 25.0 cm³).
• **Boiling tube / test tube** — small-scale reactions and heating.

**Heating and evaporating:**
• **Bunsen burner** — adjustable gas flame; blue (roaring) for heating, yellow (safety) when not in use.
• **Tripod and gauze** — supports a beaker above a Bunsen burner; gauze spreads the heat.
• **Evaporating basin** — wide, shallow dish for evaporating solvents to obtain a solid.
• **Crucible** — withstands high temperatures for strong heating.

**Separation:**
• **Filter funnel + filter paper** — separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (filtration).
• **Clamp stand, boss and clamp** — holds equipment securely at the required height.

**Choosing equipment:** Use a measuring cylinder for volumes accurate to ±0.5 cm³, a burette or pipette when higher accuracy is needed, and a beaker only for approximate measurements.

theory_blocks.title: Hazard symbols and safety precautions
theory_blocks.body:
**GHS hazard symbols** (red-bordered diamonds) warn about chemical dangers:

• **Flammable** (flame symbol) — catches fire easily. Keep away from flames; no naked flames near flammable solvents.
• **Corrosive** (liquid pouring on hand/surface) — destroys skin and metals. Wear gloves and eye protection.
• **Toxic** (skull and crossbones) — can cause death or serious harm even in small amounts. Avoid skin contact, do not inhale.
• **Harmful / Irritant** (exclamation mark) — can cause irritation or moderate harm. Wear eye protection, wash hands.
• **Oxidising** (flame over circle) — provides oxygen to help other things burn. Keep away from flammable materials.
• **Environmental hazard** (dead tree/fish) — harmful to aquatic life. Do not pour down the drain.

**General safety rules:**
1. Always wear safety goggles when heating or using chemicals.
2. Tie back long hair; tuck in ties.
3. Never eat or drink in the laboratory.
4. Point test tubes away from yourself and others when heating.
5. Waft gases toward your nose — never sniff directly.
6. Know the location of the fire extinguisher, fire blanket and eye wash station.
7. Report spills and breakages immediately.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing the right equipment
theory_blocks.body:
**Question:** You need to add exactly 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid to a conical flask. Which piece of equipment should you use to measure this volume?

**Answer:** A **pipette** (25.0 cm³ grade). A pipette delivers a single fixed volume with high accuracy.

**Why not other equipment?**
• A beaker is too imprecise — its markings are only approximate.
• A measuring cylinder could give ±0.5 cm³ accuracy, but the question asks for exactly 25.0 cm³.
• A burette could deliver 25.0 cm³ but is better suited to adding variable volumes (as in a titration).

**Rule of thumb:** For a fixed, precise volume → pipette. For a variable, precise volume → burette. For approximate volumes → measuring cylinder.

keywords.definition: A long graduated glass tube with a tap, used to deliver precise variable volumes of liquid. Accurate to ±0.05 cm³.
A piece of equipment that delivers a fixed, precise volume of liquid (e.g. 25.0 cm³).
A warning symbol on a chemical container showing the type of danger (flammable, corrosive, toxic, etc.).
The curved surface of a liquid in a tube. Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level for an accurate measurement.

worked_examples.statement: A student wants to separate sand from salt water. Describe the equipment and steps needed.
knowns: Mixture of sand and salt water
Sand is insoluble, salt is dissolved
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: **Filtration** — pour the mixture through **filter paper** in a **filter funnel** supported by a **clamp stand**. The sand stays on the filter paper (residue); the salt solution passes through (filtrate).
Step 2: **Evaporation** — pour the filtrate into an **evaporating basin**. Heat gently using a **Bunsen burner** on a **tripod and gauze** until crystals start to form. Then leave to cool and crystallise.

Equipment needed: filter funnel, filter paper, clamp stand, beaker (to collect filtrate), evaporating basin, Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze, safety goggles.
worked_examples.interpretation: Filtration separates insoluble solids; evaporation separates dissolved solids from a solution.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Heating the evaporating basin to dryness with a strong flame — this can cause spitting and produces poor-quality crystals.

worked_examples.statement: A bottle of concentrated sulfuric acid has a corrosive hazard symbol. State two safety precautions you should take when using it.
worked_examples.solution:
1. Wear safety goggles to protect the eyes from splashes.
2. Wear chemical-resistant gloves to protect the skin.
Additional: work in a well-ventilated area, know the location of the eye wash station, add acid to water (never water to acid) to avoid violent spattering.
worked_examples.interpretation: Corrosive chemicals destroy living tissue and metals. PPE (personal protective equipment) is the first line of defence.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Pouring water into concentrated acid — always add acid to water to prevent a dangerous exothermic reaction at the surface.

exercises.statement: Name the piece of equipment used to: (a) measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of a solution, (b) heat a liquid gently, (c) measure variable volumes accurately during a titration.
exercises.answer: (a) Pipette. (b) Bunsen burner (with tripod and gauze). (c) Burette.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A pipette delivers a fixed, precise volume. (b) A Bunsen burner, with the liquid in a beaker on a tripod and gauze, provides gentle heating. (c) A burette delivers variable volumes from a tap, read to ±0.05 cm³.

common_errors.correction: A measuring cylinder is less precise (±0.5 cm³). For exactly 25.0 cm³, a pipette is needed.

exercises.statement: Name the hazard symbol that warns a chemical: (a) catches fire easily, (b) can destroy skin and metals, (c) can cause death in small amounts.
exercises.answer: (a) Flammable. (b) Corrosive. (c) Toxic.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Flammable — flame symbol. (b) Corrosive — liquid pouring on hand/surface. (c) Toxic — skull and crossbones.

common_errors.correction: Toxic = serious harm or death. Harmful/irritant = moderate harm or irritation.

exercises.statement: A student wants to heat 50 cm³ of a solution to boiling in a school laboratory. Describe the equipment setup she should use and one safety precaution.
exercises.answer: Place the solution in a beaker on a gauze mat supported by a tripod. Heat from below using a Bunsen burner with a blue flame. Safety precaution: wear safety goggles in case of splashing.
exercises.full_solution: Equipment: beaker (to hold solution), tripod (support), gauze (to spread heat evenly), Bunsen burner (heat source), heatproof mat (underneath). Safety: wear goggles, point the beaker away from people, do not leave unattended, use a blue (roaring) flame for efficient heating.

common_errors.error: Heating directly in a measuring cylinder
common_errors.correction: Never heat a measuring cylinder — it is made of thin glass and will crack. Transfer the liquid to a beaker first.

exercises.statement: Name the piece of apparatus you would use to: (a) measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of liquid, (b) heat a liquid gently, (c) transfer a small amount of solid, (d) measure temperature.
exercises.answer: (a) Pipette (25 cm³). (b) Bunsen burner (with tripod and gauze, or water bath). (c) Spatula. (d) Thermometer.

exercises.statement: State three general safety rules for working in a chemistry laboratory.
exercises.answer: 1. Always wear safety goggles when handling chemicals or heating substances. 2. Never taste or directly smell chemicals. 3. Report any spills or breakages to the teacher immediately.

exercises.statement: Describe the correct procedure for heating a liquid in a test tube over a Bunsen burner.
exercises.answer: Hold the test tube at an angle (about 45°) using a test tube holder. Point the mouth of the test tube away from yourself and others. Gently heat the liquid by moving the test tube in and out of the flame, heating from the top of the liquid down to avoid bumping (sudden boiling).

challenge_questions.statement:
A student needs to measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for a titration.
(a) Name the most suitable piece of equipment for this measurement and explain why it is better than a measuring cylinder. (2 marks)
(b) Describe two safety precautions the student should take when handling the acid. (2 marks)
(c) The student accidentally spills some acid on the bench. Describe the correct procedure for dealing with this. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) A pipette (with a pipette filler) is most suitable because it measures a fixed, precise volume with a smaller uncertainty than a measuring cylinder.
(b) Any two of: wear safety goggles to protect eyes; wear a lab coat to protect clothing; use a pipette filler (never suck by mouth); handle in a well-ventilated area; keep the acid away from the bench edge.
(c) Alert the teacher. Neutralise the spill with sodium hydrogen carbonate (a weak base) to prevent further reaction, then wipe up with paper towels and wash the area with water.

challenge_questions.statement:
In an experiment to measure the volume of gas produced during a reaction:
(a) Draw and label the apparatus you would use to collect the gas over water. (3 marks)
(b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of collecting gas over water compared with using a gas syringe. (2 marks)
(c) State one variable that must be controlled to make the experiment a fair test. (1 mark)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Diagram should show: a conical flask with reactants, a delivery tube leading from the flask into a trough of water, and an inverted measuring cylinder (full of water) over the end of the delivery tube to collect the gas.
(b) Advantage: cheaper and does not require specialist equipment. Disadvantage: the gas may dissolve in water, giving an inaccurate volume reading (or: it is harder to read the volume precisely).
(c) Any one of: temperature, concentration of reactant, volume of reactant, mass of solid reactant.

challenge_questions.statement: Describe the hazard symbols for: (i) corrosive, (ii) flammable, and (iii) toxic substances. For each, give one example of a chemical used in school laboratories that carries that symbol and one precaution specific to that hazard. (6 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(i) Corrosive: symbol shows surfaces/skin being damaged by drops. Example: concentrated sulfuric acid. Precaution: wear gloves and goggles; avoid skin contact.
(ii) Flammable: symbol shows a flame. Example: ethanol. Precaution: keep away from naked flames and heat sources; use in a well-ventilated area.
(iii) Toxic: symbol shows a skull and crossbones. Example: chlorine gas. Precaution: use in a fume cupboard; avoid inhaling vapour.

mcq.stem: Which piece of equipment gives the most accurate measurement of 25.0 cm³ of liquid?

options.why_wrong: Beaker markings are only approximate — suitable for rough measurements, not precise ones.
A measuring cylinder is accurate to ±0.5 cm³, which is less precise than a pipette.
Conical flasks have no precise volume markings — they are used for mixing, not measuring.

mcq.explanation: A pipette delivers a fixed, precise volume (e.g. 25.0 cm³) with very high accuracy, making it the best choice for this measurement.

mcq.stem: What does the skull and crossbones hazard symbol warn about?

options.why_wrong: Flammable substances have a flame symbol.

options.text: The substance is toxic — it can cause death or serious harm

options.why_wrong: Corrosive substances have a symbol showing liquid pouring on a hand and surface.
Irritants have an exclamation mark (!) symbol.

mcq.explanation: The skull and crossbones symbol warns that the substance is toxic — it can cause death or serious harm even in small amounts.

mcq.stem: Which equipment would you use to deliver variable, precise volumes of an acid during a titration?

options.why_wrong: A pipette delivers a fixed volume. In a titration, the pipette measures the alkali, and the burette delivers the acid.
A measuring cylinder is not precise enough for titration work (±0.5 cm³ vs ±0.05 cm³).
A beaker has only approximate markings — it cannot deliver precise volumes.

mcq.explanation: A burette has a tap that allows variable volumes to be delivered precisely (accurate to ±0.05 cm³). It is the standard equipment for titrations.

mcq.stem: When heating a liquid in a boiling tube, the open end should be pointed:

options.why_wrong: If the liquid spits or boils over, it could burn you.
This puts others at risk if the liquid spits.
Holding it vertically increases the chance of liquid shooting out of the top when heated. Angle it away from people.

mcq.explanation: Always point the open end of a boiling tube away from yourself and others. Hot liquids can spit or boil over unexpectedly.

exam_notes.note: You may be asked to draw equipment diagrams. Learn the standard cross-section shapes: beaker, flask, funnel, burette.
Questions about hazard symbols often ask you to name the symbol AND give a precaution — always give both.
In 'describe the method' questions, name specific equipment (not just 'a container' — say 'a 100 cm³ beaker').

summary.big_idea: Choosing the right equipment and following safety rules are essential practical skills. Match the equipment to the precision needed and know the hazard symbols.
key_points: Pipette for fixed precise volumes; burette for variable precise volumes; measuring cylinder for approximate volumes.
Know the six main GHS hazard symbols and their meanings.
Read the meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Always wear safety goggles when heating or handling chemicals.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Pipette = fixed precise. Burette = variable precise. Know your hazard symbols. Goggles on.
